title: Strat Chat Questioning
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien offers a practical framework for classroom questioning by distinguishing closed and open questions and identifying four types of bad teacher questions. His classroom observations found one teacher asking 115 questions per 60-minute lesson and another asking only 8 -- with quality differences just as stark as quantity. Brien rehabilitates closed questions, which were demonized in his teacher education, arguing they are indispensable diagnostic tools for checking understanding before introducing complexity. He shows how a closed question can be instantly converted to open with a follow-up 'and why is that the case?' The article identifies four bad teacher questions: asking about untaught content, 'does this make sense?', 'any questions?', and confidence ratings. Brien's core argument is that the right combination of closed and open questions both checks whether instruction was effective and creates pathways to deeper thinking.
points: Closed questions -- despite being demonized in teacher education -- are excellent diagnostic tools for checking understanding of individual elements before introducing complexity; a student cannot answer a question about a topic's implications if they don't know its basic content.
A closed question can be instantly converted to open by appending 'and why is that the case?' -- this transforms a yes/no check into an extended explanation with almost no teacher preparation cost.
'Does this make sense?' and 'Any questions?' are structurally questions but functionally useless for checking understanding because they invite social compliance rather than cognitive engagement.

Open questions carry a real trade-off: they require more time and impose greater cognitive load on the teacher (who must process up to 25 different responses) -- the decision to use them should be deliberate.

Brien's observation that one teacher asked 115 questions in 60 minutes while another asked only 8 dramatizes how radically different classroom practice can be on a dimension that rarely receives explicit professional attention.
quotes: In class one the questions were almost all directly related to the content being taught. There was a significant number of closed questions about the topic either posed to all students or individual students called upon to respond and then some open questions requiring longer form responses as the class progressed.

In class two however the majority of questions were along the lines of 'any questions?' and 'does that make sense?' which are far less effective indicators of student understanding despite the fact that structurally they are a question.

Despite the way they were demonized in my graduate diploma in education I use closed questions constantly in my classes. Why? Well they're an incredible diagnostic tool as a check for understanding before delving into more challenging open questions.

A closed question also does not need to remain closed. Much like the sign on the front of a convenience store it takes but a moment to switch it around to open when gaining a students closed response by hitting them with a 'and why is that the case?'

During my university studies it was posed to our cohort that we should mainly be asking open questions in our lessons if we want our students to be 'thinking deeply' and while that deep thought is incredibly important, if we do not first ascertain what the students know through closed questions we may just end up with a class of students staring blankly at a page.

Even when we do move towards asking open questions, we do not do this too flippantly. We must hasten slowly and first model to students how to go through the process of responding to similar open questions before gradually releasing control to minimize the potential of the cursed blank page remaining.
